chunks: What a DMM can measure. The question: What can it measure?
A multimeter does far more than read voltage. Besides DC and AC voltage, current and resistance, it usually has continuity (a beeper for "is this path connected?")
, a diode test, capacitance, frequency and temperature. The useful skill is knowing how each function works inside and where it can give a confident wrong number.
Think of a Swiss Army knife. One handle carries a blade, scissors and a screwdriver, and each tool is fine for its job.
But the scissors are not a good saw, and the little blade is not a good cleaver. A multimeter's extra functions work the same way.
They are handy for quick checks, but a dedicated instrument is more accurate.
three waveforms with the same peak value have different RMS values because of how long they spend near the peak. A meter that assumes a sine wave mis-scales the others.
RMS: the "effective" size of an AC signal, the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally. True-RMS meter: computes the real RMS of any waveform shape.
Average-responding meter: flips negative parts positive, averages, and scales the result as if the wave were a sine. It is only right for sine waves.
Continuity: a quick check of whether a path has low resistance, usually with a beeper.
Diode test: the meter pushes a small current through a diode and shows its voltage drop, about 0. 6 volts for a silicon diode.
Measure a symmetric square wave that swings between +5 volts and -5 volts. Its true RMS value is exactly 5. 00 volts, because it sits at full height all the time.
A true-RMS meter reads 5. 00 volts. An average-responding meter flips the negative half positive and averages it: 5 volts. It then multiplies by 1.
11, the factor that is correct for a sine wave, and shows 5. 55 volts. That is 11% too high. Same signal, two different readings, and only one is right. That is the whole idea.
"A DMM measures DC and AC voltage, DC and AC current and resistance, plus continuity, diode test, usually capacitance, frequency and duty cycle, and temperature with a thermocouple.
For AC I want true-RMS, because an average-responding meter is only right for sine waves.

Limits to remember: 10 megohm input loads high-impedance nodes, current ranges add burden voltage and need the right jack and fuse, resistance should be measured out of circuit, and AC and frequency functions only work up to a limited bandwidth."
